summary: This note covers the 1859 State of the Union Address, written by President James Buchanan and read to both houses of the 36th United States Congress on Monday, December 19, 1859, by a clerk. In it Buchanan addresses the recent violence at Harpers Ferry and warns that such events may be symptoms of an incurable disease in the public mind that could end in open war over slavery. The note includes a direct quotation from the address.
one_line: James Buchanan's December 1859 State of the Union Address, which warned of civil war over slavery after the Harpers Ferry raid.
key_facts: The 1859 State of the Union Address was written by James Buchanan, the 15th President of the United States.
The address was read to both houses of the 36th United States Congress on Monday, December 19, 1859.
The address was read by a clerk rather than delivered in person by the President.
Buchanan wrote that he would not refer in detail to the recent sad and bloody occurrences at Harpers Ferry.
Buchanan described the Harpers Ferry events as bad and cruel in themselves.
Buchanan said the Harpers Ferry events derived their chief importance from the apprehension that they were symptoms of an incurable disease in the public mind.
Buchanan warned that the disease might break out in still more dangerous outrages.
Buchanan warned that the disease might terminate at last in an open war by the North to abolish slavery in the South.
The address is described as predicting the American Civil War.
